title: Deal Cards Into Straight Runs
statement:
Each card in cards shows a whole number. You want to split all the cards into groups of exactly k cards, where the values in each group are k consecutive numbers, such as 7, 8, 9 for k = 3. Every card goes into exactly one group, and the same value may appear on several cards.

Return true if such a split exists, otherwise false.

examples.why: 3, 4, 5 and 6, 7, 8. The input order does not matter.
10, 11, 12 and 11, 12, 13. The runs overlap, so the two 11s and the two 12s must go into different groups. Looking only at distinct values (10 to 13) would say false.
Six cards split evenly into groups of 3, but once 4, 5, 6 is taken, the second group 6, 7, … needs an 8. A count check alone is not enough.

hints: Look at the smallest card. Which group can it belong to?
Nothing smaller exists, so the smallest card must be the first card of its run. Its whole run is forced.
Count the cards per value. Visit values in increasing order; if value x still has c cards left, it starts c runs, so x + 1 … x + k − 1 each need at least c cards. Subtract and continue.

explain.intuition:
The smallest card has no choice. A run containing it cannot start lower, because there is no lower card, so it must start the run x, x + 1, …, x + k − 1. Taking that run is not a guess: every valid split contains it. Remove those cards and the same argument applies to the new smallest card. A greedy rule that is forced at every step can never lead you astray.

Doing this one card at a time is slow, so work with counts. Visit the distinct values in increasing order. If value x still has c cards when you reach it, all c of them are the smallest cards left, so all c start a run. Each of the next k − 1 values must have at least c cards to give; subtract c from each. If one falls short, the answer is false.
steps: If cards.length is not a multiple of k, return false.
Count how many cards show each value.
Go through the distinct values in increasing order. Let c be the count left for value x; skip it if c = 0.
For each v from x to x + k − 1: if count[v] < c, return false; otherwise count[v] −= c.
pitfalls: Checking only that the length divides by k. Example 3 passes that test and still fails.
Working with distinct values. Duplicates must land in different runs, as in example 2.
Sorting numbers with JavaScript's default sort(), which compares them as strings: 10 comes before 9, and the "smallest" card is wrong.

complexity.time: O(n log n) for sorting the distinct values

solutions.title: Pull the smallest card's run, one card at a time
solutions.idea: Sort the cards. Repeatedly take the smallest card and remove one card of each of the next k − 1 values, searching the list each time.

solutions.title: Counts, smallest value first
solutions.idea: Count each value. In increasing order, a value with c cards left starts c runs, so the next k − 1 values each give up c cards.

followups: Do it without sorting: how can you find the start of a run from any value by walking down from it?
Runs may now have any length of at least k. Which greedy choice do you make for each card?
